paper.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project number is given. The article states only that 'An Online Appendix for this article can be found at QJE online (qje.oxfordjournals.org)' (p. 1216).

sample frame; controls (age, gender, marital status, partner status)

registers.name_in_paper: the Danish Integrated Database for Labor Market Research (IDA)
registers.role: treatment construction: firm identifiers used to define firm switches and mass layoffs

linkages: individuals linked across the income tax register, the population register and IDA to form an annual panel for the Danish population 1995-2009
workers linked to firms via IDA firm identifiers (missing in 2003, 2005 and 2007, when the identifiers were changed)
individuals linked to partners (married, cohabiting with a common child, or cohabiting opposite-gender adults within 15 years of age who are not blood relatives)

sample.universe: The Danish population aged 18-60 without self-employment income, 1995-2009
sample.unit_of_observation: person-year (person-by-firm-switch in the employer pension analysis)
selection_rules: start from the population data set, 1995-2009
exclude observations in which individuals are below age 18 or over 60

for the employer pension analysis: keep individuals with earnings from two distinct firms in year t and t-1; drop switches in which earnings fell by more than half or more than doubled (about 25% of switches); firm-switch status is missing in 2003, 2005 and 2007
for the MSP analysis: keep individuals with 1998 labor income within DKr 25,000 of the DKr 34,500 cutoff; drop 401 doctoral students earning exactly DKr 49,987.50
for the subsidy analysis: keep observations with taxable income within DKr 75,000 of the top tax cutoff, 1996-2001
sample.n_observations: 41,159,806 (approximately 41 million); 16,457,106 in the top tax threshold sample
sample.n_individuals: 4,001,015 (approximately 4 million); 1,345,753 in the top tax threshold sample

construction_notes: All monetary values are reported in nominal Danish kroner; the exchange rate was approximately DKr 6.5 per US$1 over the period.
Pension contribution levels are top-coded at the 99th percentile in each account in each year.
Taxable savings measures and all pension contribution rates (as a percentage of income) are trimmed at the 1st and 99th percentiles of the relevant estimation sample.
Taxable saving S is the change in end-of-year nonpension assets; it excludes home equity, mortgage debt, durables, cash outside bank accounts and exotic assets.
Net saving is gross saving minus the change in nonmortgage liabilities.
Total saving is defined as S^tot_it = P^E_it + P^I_it + S_it/(1 - MTR_it), that is, pension contributions plus taxable saving measured in pretax dollars.
Labor income Y is pretax wage earnings excluding employer-administered pension contributions; total compensation W adds employer pension contributions; taxable income Ytax adds other taxable income.
The employer-provided pension contribution P^E is the sum of the employer portion and the compulsory worker portion of the employer-administered plan.
Taxable saving in the subsidy analysis is measured in pretax dollars as S/(1 - 0.6), using the 60% marginal tax rate in the top bracket.
Mass layoffs are defined as more than 90% of workers leaving a firm with at least 50 employees within a single year, with no more than 50% of the original employees ending up at the same new firm.
All income and savings variables are third-party reported by employers, pension funds, banks and financial institutions.

links.pointer_quote: Most individuals do not change voluntary pension contributions, savings in taxable accounts, or liabilities at all when they switch to firms that contribute more to their retirement account, consistent with passive behavior.

population.selection: Conditioned on switching firms; observations whose earnings fell by more than half or more than doubled are excluded; Panels A and B further condition on being in the interior of the choice set (positive lagged individual pension contributions, or lagged wealth above 10% of labor income); individuals with Delta w < -50% or > 100% and, within that group, those with Delta p^E or Delta s^tot in the top or bottom 1% are excluded.

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic changes in employer-provided pension contribution rates when workers switch firms, 1995-2009; firms' contribution rates differ because of collective bargaining agreements.

key_assumptions.assumption: Cov(epsilon^E_i, Delta p^E_i) = 0: changes in employer pension contributions at a firm switch are orthogonal to unobserved determinants of the change in savings rates, conditional on the change in total compensation.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The paper argues job changes generate high-frequency changes in employer pensions that are plausibly orthogonal to tastes for saving, and tests this with the mass-layoff subsample (Table III, column (3)) and the absence of a pre-trend in Figure I, Panel A.

lhs: Delta p^E (change in employer pension contribution rate)
rhs: epsilon^E (unobserved determinants of the change in savings rates)

implies_edges.from: Delta w (change in total compensation)

key_assumptions.assumption: An individual's preferences for saving would not have jumped sharply in year 0 in the absence of the change in firm pension policies (no anticipation / no coincident taste shock at the switch).
key_assumptions.supported_by: No trend toward higher individual pension contributions before year 0 in Figure I, Panel A; Figure I, Panel D shows the propensity to adjust individual contributions rises by only 21% at a switch to a much higher-contributing firm.

implies_edges.from: Delta p^E (change in employer pension contribution rate)
implies_edges.to: individual pension contributions before the switch

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is restricted to individuals in the interior of the choice set (positive lagged individual pension contributions, or lagged wealth above 10% of labor income), so that pass-through reflects behaviour rather than a mechanical corner.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated as a sample restriction in the text and in the notes to Table III; the paper also reports the corner-free threshold approach in Panel C as a check.

implies_edges.from: lagged individual pension contributions / lagged wealth above 10% of labor income

key_assumptions.assumption: Two-type (binary) response: individuals either fully offset the change in P^E to the extent possible or make no change at all, so the estimated pass-through rate phi_E equals 1 minus the fraction of active savers alpha_E.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Asserted in Section II and supported by Figure I, Panel D, which shows most individuals leave individual pension contributions literally unchanged.

threats_discussed: endogenous sorting of workers into firms with higher pension contributions (addressed with the mass-layoff subsample in column (3))
corners in the individual pension and taxable saving choice sets (addressed by the sample restriction and by the threshold approach in Panel C)
resource pooling within couples (addressed in Online Appendix Table I)
unobserved home equity and mortgage debt (addressed on the subsample of renters)
robustness_checks: mass-layoff subsample (column (3))
top tax cutoff subsample (column (4))
net saving instead of gross saving (column (5))
first firm switch only (column (6))
adding age, gender, marital status, college and two-digit occupation controls (Panel B)
threshold approach that is unaffected by corners (Panel C)
renters, household-level saving and individuals without partners (Online Appendix Table I)
unresolved_confounders: home equity wealth and mortgage debt are not observed, so investments in home improvements and payments to home equity are missed
investments in other durables such as cars or appliances are not captured
cash holdings outside bank accounts and exotic assets are excluded from the wealth data

estimation.clustering: by the firm to which the individual switches

first firm switch only

definition.value: The change in the employer-provided pension contribution rate (employer plus the compulsory worker portion of the employer-administered plan) from the year before to the year of a firm switch, measured as a percentage of labor income in the year before the switch.

timing.value: change from event year t = -1 to event year t = 0 around a firm switch

register_source.value: income tax register (third-party-reported pension contributions and earnings from employers and pension funds); income tax register (third-party-reported end-of-year assets and liabilities from banks and financial institutions)

definition.value: The change in the total savings rate, Delta s^tot, where total saving is S^tot_{it} = P^E_{it} + P^I_{it} + S_{it}/(1 - MTR_{it}): employer plus individual pension contributions plus taxable saving measured in pretax dollars, expressed as a percentage of labor income in the year before the switch.

timing.value: change from event year t = -1 to event year t = 0 around a firm switch
